```c
6256                          (struct sockaddr *) &peer, &peerlen);
6257
6258    if (pg_atomic_read_u32(&ic_control_info.shutdown) == 1)   // safe: plain volatile load
...
6267    if (DEBUG5 >= log_min_messages)                          // <-- runs BEFORE errno check
6268        write_log("received inbound len %d", read_count);
6269
6270    if (read_count < 0)
6271    {
6272        skip_poll = false;
6273
6274        if (errno == EWOULDBLOCK || errno == EINTR)          // reads possibly-clobbered errno
6275            continue;
6276
6277        write_log("Interconnect error: recvfrom (%d)", errno);
6278        setRxThreadError(errno);                              // latches a permanent error
```

`recvfrom()` sets `errno` on failure, but before it's checked at line 6274, a conditional `write_log(...)` call at 6267–6268 can run. `write_log()` (`cdbthreadlog.c`) internally calls `gettimeofday`, `pthread_mutex_lock/unlock`, `vfprintf`, and `fflush(stderr)` — none of which are guaranteed to preserve `errno`. This matches the reported symptom exactly.

The `write_log` is gated on `DEBUG5 >= log_min_messages` (DEBUG5=10 in `elog.h`, so it only fires when interconnect debug logging is turned all the way up) — which is why it's *sporadic*: it only manifests when verbose debug logging is enabled, ironically often exactly when someone is investigating interconnect flakiness.

## Root cause

**What changed:** commit `09a6167597f` ("back up pg_stat to heap table", the ancestor of `pg_stat_backup.c`) turned the stats collector from PostgreSQL's classic "fire-and-forget UDP listener" into a **fully participating backend**. `PgstatCollectorMain()` (`src/backend/postmaster/pgstat.c:5642`) now calls `InitProcess()` and `InitPostgres("postgres", ...)`, so the collector gets a real `PGPROC`, joins the `ProcArray`, and — critically — `InitProcess()` calls `SwitchToSharedLatch()` (`src/backend/storage/lmgr/proc.c:627`), which repoints `MyLatch` from the process-**local** latch to the **shared** `MyProc->procLatch`.

That repointing matters because the collector's main loop still waits like this (`pgstat.c:5964-5967`):

```c
wr = WaitLatchOrSocket(MyLatch,
                       WL_LATCH_SET | WL_POSTMASTER_DEATH | WL_SOCKET_READABLE,
                       pgStatSock, -1L,   /* <-- infinite timeout, non-Windows */
                       WAIT_EVENT_PGSTAT_MAIN);
```

With a **local** latch (the pre-existing design), `-1L` is safe: the only things that can ever set that latch are the collector's own signal handlers running in-process (`pgstat_sighup_handler`, `pgstat_exit`), plus new UDP traffic on `pgStatSock`. Every wakeup path is guaranteed to fire.

Once the latch became **shared**, arbitrary other backends can legitimately call `SetLatch(&collectorProc->procLatch)` as part of normal Postgres machinery the collector now participates in as a real backend (heavyweight-lock/group-XID wakeups, condition variables, ProcSignal-based interrupts, etc.). Cross-process `SetLatch()` (`src/backend/storage/ipc/latch.c:490-491`) does **not** touch the target's self-pipe directly — it only does `kill(owner_pid, SIGUSR1)` and relies on the target's own `SIGUSR1` handler to write to its self-pipe (`latch_sigusr1_handler()`, `latch.c:1594`), which is the only thing that can actually break the target out of its blocking `epoll_wait()/poll()`.

The bug (tracked as **#1846**): at the point `PgstatCollectorMain` was converted to use `InitProcess()`, the signal setup was left untouched:

```c
pqsignal(SIGUSR1, SIG_IGN);
```

`SIG_IGN` means the kernel discards the signal before it can ever interrupt the blocking syscall — no `EINTR`, nothing written to the self-pipe. The shared `Latch.is_set` flag does get flipped by the setter, but the collector, already parked in `WaitLatchOrSocket(..., -1L, ...)`, never notices. It only ever wakes up again by pure chance, when some other backend happens to send a new stats UDP datagram on `pgStatSock`. If a backend is meanwhile blocked waiting on something that only resolves once the collector runs its next loop iteration (e.g. it's queued behind a heavyweight lock the collector holds during the `relyt_stats_backup` catalog DML in `BackupPgStat()` → `DoBackup()` → `UpdateRelytStatsBackup()`, `contrib/zdb/src/storage/pg_stat_backup.c:314-375`, which takes `RowExclusiveLock` via `heap_open()`), that backend can wait indefinitely — exactly the "block indefinitely" symptom.

## Current state

This exact bug was already partially fixed on this branch by commit `34fbfd18354` ("fix #1846: process SIGUSR1 in pgstat after InitPostgres()", already an ancestor of HEAD): it adds `pgstat_sigusr1_handler()` calling `latch_sigusr1_handler()` and installs it in place of `SIG_IGN`. That closes the specific hole above.

## Remaining gap / proposed hardening

The design is still fragile because it depends on *every* future code path that can set the collector's shared latch reliably delivering and handling `SIGUSR1` — a single regression (or a signal-blocked critical section at the wrong instant) reproduces the same indefinite hang, and there's no self-healing. ## Pipeline (confirmed)

```
DROP TABLE → SetFlagForDroppingTable (zdb_aocsam.c:6020) writes a WORK-space tombstone in FDB
    ↓ (driven by autovacuum, contrib/zdb/src/zdb.c:5695 → VacuumDroppedRelations)
zdb_vacuum.c:7213 VacuumDroppedRelations()
  ├─ BackupDroppedRelations()  → GetDroppedRelations(WORK)   → DispatchBackupTaskForDroppedTable
  └─ GCDroppedRelations()      → GetDroppedRelations(BACKUP) → DispatchGCTaskForDroppedTable
```

Both stages loop `for (shardid = 0; shardid < totalShardNum; ++shardid)`, where `totalShardNum = GetZDBShardNumByRelfilenode(relfilenode)` (`zdb_shard_stats.c:537`) — this just scans `zdb_shard_stats` **rows currently present** for that relfilenode and returns `max(shardid)+1` (verified at `zdb_shard_stats.c:560-573`; the scan key is only on `relfilenode`, it doesn't care about `relid`).

There's deliberately no retention window here (`deletedBackupInterval/deletedGCInterval = 0`, hardcoded at `zdb_vacuum.c:6696`/`:6977`) — that part is intentional (fixed previously in commit `d3aedae9cfd`), so it's not the bug.

## Root cause: a one-way "shard-count ratchet" in the BACKUP post-commit path

In the autovacuum post-commit hook, the BACKUP-task branch (`zdb_vacuum.c:2962-3011`) does this **every round**:

```c
// zdb_vacuum.c:2974-2986
if (!OidIsValid(currentVacuumTaskTxnRelid) && OidIsValid(currentVacuumTaskTxnRelfilenode))
{
    RemoveZDBShardStatsByRefilenode(currentVacuumTaskTxnRelfilenode, false);   // unconditional
}
for (int i = 0; i < currentTaskTxnShardStatsNum; ++i)
    UpdateZDBShardStatsByBackupTask(&currentTaskTxnShardStats[i]);            // only reported shards
```

`RemoveZDBShardStatsByRefilenode(relfilenode, false)` (`zdb_shard_stats.c:382-429`) deletes **all** rows for that relfilenode with `relid > InvalidOid` — i.e. every shard's leftover "live" stats row from before the drop — regardless of which shards actually succeeded this round. `currentTaskTxnShardStats[]` is populated in `HandleBackupTaskResultForDroppedTable` (`zdb_vacuum.c:6758-6858`) strictly from QE results with `PGRES_TUPLES_OK`/`PGRES_COMMAND_OK` (`:6783-6794` — any other status just `elog(WARNING); continue`s, silently dropping that shard for this round).

**Net effect:** on the first backup round after a DROP, if any single shard's dispatch/report fails for an ordinary transient reason (segment blip, gmeta hiccup, timeout) — more likely on a large, multi-shard table needing many rounds to drain — its old row is deleted and **never reinserted**, because nothing else ever recreates a shard_stats row except a successful round for that exact shard. If the shard that's lost happens to be the current highest shard id, `GetZDBShardNumByRelfilenode` permanently returns a smaller `totalShardNum` next round, so `GenerateBackupTaskForDroppedTable`'s loop (`zdb_vacuum.c:6725`) never iterates that shard index again. GC mirrors the same `totalShardNum` computation, so it never looks for that shard's BACKUP-space files either. gmeta correctly refuses to clear the tombstone while files remain (this is the invariant `d3aedae9cfd` established), so `GetDroppedRelations` re-surfaces the relfilenode **forever** — matching exactly the "large table, lingers indefinitely" symptom.

The GC-task branch (`zdb_vacuum.c:3013-3057`) does **not** have this flaw — it only deletes shard_stats rows once `CheckDroppedRelationsExist` confirms via gmeta that both FDB spaces are truly empty (`:3033-3038`). That's the safe pattern the BACKUP branch should follow.

## Proposed fix

The blanket delete exists because `UpdateZDBShardStatsByBackupTask` looks up rows by `(relid=InvalidOid, relfilenode, shardid)` (`zdb_shard_stats.c:232-237`), so it can never find/replace the *old* row still keyed by the real pre-drop `relid` — hence the "delete everything, then reinsert only what we have" approach. The fix is to scope the delete to exactly the shards being reinserted this round, not the whole relfilenode:

1. Add a shard-scoped variant, e.g. `RemoveZDBShardStatsByRefilenodeAndShard(Oid relFileNode, int16 shardid, bool dropped)` in `zdb_shard_stats.c`, by adding a third `ScanKeyInit` on `Anum_zdb_shard_stats_shardid` to the existing `RemoveZDBShardStatsByRefilenode` scan (`zdb_shard_stats.c:404-422`).
2. In `zdb_vacuum.c:2974-2986`, drop the unconditional relfilenode-wide `RemoveZDBShardStatsByRefilenode(..., false)` call. Instead, inside the `for (int i = 0; i < currentTaskTxnShardStatsNum; ++i)` loop, call the new per-shard delete for `currentTaskTxnShardStats[i].shardid` immediately before `UpdateZDBShardStatsByBackupTask(&currentTaskTxnShardStats[i])`.

This means a shard whose round fails simply keeps its old (stale-relid) row untouched — `GetZDBShardNumByRelfilenode` still counts it (it doesn't filter by relid), so it's retried next round exactly like today's "no throttle" design intends, and gets properly converted to a `relid=InvalidOid` row once it actually succeeds.

For a "nonexistent relation" OID in a ZDB regression test, don't just grab a small round number — a few things can bite you:

**What to pick:** Use a large constant clearly outside any range the test run could ever allocate — something like `2147483647` (INT32_MAX, still a valid `oid` since `oid` is unsigned) or `4000000000`. Cast it explicitly as `::oid` (or whatever the function's actual parameter type is), not `::regclass` — if the parameter type is `regclass`, PostgreSQL validates the OID exists *during the cast itself* and throws `ERROR: relation with OID ... does not exist` before your function ever runs. That may be the exact behavior you want to test, but if you're trying to exercise the *function's own* not-found handling, you need a raw `oid`/`int4` literal so the cast succeeds and the function gets to do its own lookup.

**What to avoid:**

1. **Small OIDs (< 16384 / `FirstNormalObjectId`)** — these are reserved for objects created by `initdb` (system catalogs, types, etc.). A hardcoded small number like `1`, `100`, or `1259` risks accidentally *matching a real system object* rather than testing "doesn't exist," making the test meaningless or non-portable across PG/GPDB versions.
2. **OID `0`** — that's `InvalidOid`, and many code paths special-case it as "not specified" rather than "not found," so it exercises a different branch than a genuine nonexistent-but-well-formed OID.
3. **Assuming "OID" means `pg_class.oid`** — verify this against the actual C function signature first. Per this repo's own testing conventions (see CLAUDE.md's regression-test guidance), several ZDB introspection UDFs (`zdb_get_metainfo_for_file`, `zdb_get_metainfo_for_drop_flag`, `zdb_get_metainfo_for_visimap`) key off **`relfilenode`**, not `pg_class.oid` — those are different values. If the function you're testing is one of these, double-check which one the parameter actually is before hardcoding anything.
4. **Test-order fragility in a shared schedule** — this repo's regress schedule runs tests against a shared cluster/FDB instance, and OIDs are handed out from a single ascending counter (in GPDB, synced across coordinator + segments). A fixed huge constant is safe in practice because the counter only grows from wherever the cluster started — it won't ever climb into the billions during a test run — but don't pick something "currently unused" that's only slightly larger than what today's schedule happens to allocate, since adding tests later could eventually reach it.

**More robust alternative:** if you don't need a literal for a byte-exact expected `.out` file, derive the OID dynamically instead of hardcoding — e.g. create a throwaway table, capture its OID, then drop it (guarantees non-existence right up until the moment you use it, and guarantees no collision regardless of what else the shared schedule has allocated). So `postgresql.auto.conf` gets updated everywhere, but only the coordinator gets the SIGHUP that makes the new value live. Segment postmasters — where ZDB's autovacuum/merge/GC workers actually run, since that's where the columnar data lives — keep whatever stale `relyt.autovacuum` value was already in memory until something else SIGHUPs them.

That's exactly why it's *occasional*: whether a given segment still has a stale "on" in memory (and whether a worker there happens to fire during your test window) depends on what earlier tests in the schedule did to that segment's config, not on your test's own setup step.

This repo already has the correct idiom for a cluster-wide reload, used elsewhere (`contrib/zdb/regress/sql/all_type.sql:3`, `shard_level_parallel.sql:6`, `explain_dispatch2swift.sql:3`, and the union form in `contrib/zdb/perf/test_autovacuum_backup_gc.py:27`):

```sql
select pg_reload_conf();
select pg_reload_conf() from gp_dist_random('gp_id');
```

Confirmed by reading `zdb_vacuum.c` and the existing `drop_table_left_meta.sql` test — here's what's actually happening.

## Why it's still flaky

**1. The GUC is checked once per decision, not polled during execution.** `gZdbAutoVacuum` (backing `relyt.autovacuum`) is only consulted inside `ZDBNeedsVacAnalyze` (`zdb_vacuum.c:1893`, `:2019`) — a single gate checked when the autovacuum worker is *deciding* whether to schedule work for a table. Once a PLAN → MERGE/BACKUP/GC pipeline for a shard has already been dispatched (including async EDPS-dispatched tasks), flipping the GUC afterward does nothing to stop it — it runs to completion. If a worker was forked or a task dispatched in the window right before your `alter system set ... off; pg_reload_conf()`, it finishes anyway.

**2. `pg_reload_conf()` alone only reloads the backend you're connected to.** In this MPP setup you need it on every segment too. The existing test does this correctly:
```sql
select * from pg_reload_conf() union all select pg_reload_conf() from gp_dist_random('gp_id');
```
A bare `select pg_reload_conf();` leaves segment-side autovacuum workers running with the old value.

**3. `relyt.autovacuum` only gates ZDB's own autovacuum logic**, not the base PostgreSQL `autovacuum` GUC. Heap-based catalog/metadata tables can still get vacuumed by the standard daemon regardless.

**4. Leakage from an earlier test in the schedule.** As the project's own testing notes point out, `alter system set` persists across tests. If the test before yours didn't `alter system reset` it, or left a `gp_inject_fault` suspend point armed, your setup can race against work that test kicked off.

**5. Global introspection scope.** Even when no GC actually touched *your* table, `zdb_get_metainfo_for_*` UDFs and `pg_catalog.zdb_*` views are cluster-wide. An unrelated table's leftover async task can make a bare `count(*)` look like GC ran against yours.

## What to do instead

Don't race the GUC + timer-driven launcher for precise "no GC happened" assertions — pin it deterministically with fault injectors, the way `drop_table_left_meta.sql` does: `gp_inject_fault('auto_vac_before_backup_dropped_table', 'suspend', ...)` before the operation, `'wait_until_triggered'` to confirm the worker actually reached (or didn't reach) that point, then `'reset'`. If you need synchronous, on-demand GC instead of waiting on autovacuum at all, drive it explicitly via `relyt_vacuum_dropped_relation()` / `relyt_vacuum_aborted_txn()`.

## Teardown checklist

```sql
-- undo every GUC you touched — reset, don't just re-set to the default value
alter system reset relyt.autovacuum;
-- ... reset any other relyt.* / autovacuum_* GUCs you set ...

-- reload on coordinator AND every segment
select * from pg_reload_conf() union all select pg_reload_conf() from gp_dist_random('gp_id');

-- reset every fault injector you armed — a lingering 'suspend' hangs
-- the NEXT test's worker if it hits the same injection point
select gp_inject_fault('<point>', 'reset', '', 'isolation2test', '', 1, 1, 0, dbid, -1)
    from gp_segment_configuration where role = 'p' and content = -1;
```

And scope any FDB-introspection assertions by `relfilenode` captured before DROP, per the existing convention — that alone would explain some of the flakiness even if GC timing were perfect.
